nameStory: The "hoary" in this willowherb's name comes from the dense covering of soft, grayish-white hairs that give the whole plant a somewhat frosted or aged appearance. "Willowherb" refers to the narrow, willow-like leaves that are characteristic of plants in this genus, though they're not related to true willows at all.
description: Hoary willowherb is a fuzzy, medium-sized perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a soft, grayish-green appearance. The entire plant is covered in fine, silky hairs that give it a distinctly velvety feel when touched. It produces small pink to purple flowers in summer and spreads by underground stems to form patches in wet areas.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Densely covered in soft, grayish-white hairs from top to bottom, giving the entire plant a distinctly fuzzy, almost silvery appearance that you can easily see and feel

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple flowers with four notched petals, about 1/4 inch across, clustered at the top of stems in a loose, branching arrangement

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem, with fine teeth along the edges and a soft, velvety texture from dense hairs

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods that split open to release tiny seeds with fluffy white hairs that catch the wind like miniature parachutes

habitat: Look for hoary willowherb in wet meadows, along stream banks, pond edges, and in marshy areas throughout New England. It prefers consistently moist to wet soils and can tolerate partial shade, often growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like sedges and rushes.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as fuzzy, grayish rosettes of leaves. The distinctive hairy coating is already apparent on young growth.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from June through August with small pink-purple flowers. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and the characteristic fuzzy appearance are most obvious.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, releasing fluffy seeds that drift on autumn breezes. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground stems. Only dried stems and empty seed pods may remain visible above ground.

funFact: Despite being called a "willowherb," this plant is actually in the evening primrose family and is more closely related to fireweed than to any willow - the name comes purely from the leaf shape resemblance!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with great willowherb, but hoary willowherb is much smaller overall and has a distinctly grayish, densely hairy appearance throughout, while great willowherb is greener with less obvious hairs and grows much taller (up to 6 feet).
contextualKnowledge: Hoary willowherb is quite rare in New England with only 5 recorded observations, making it a special find for nature enthusiasts. It's much more common in Europe and may be a naturalized species here rather than truly native.
compareHints: Among New England willowherbs, hoary willowherb stands out for its overall grayish, densely fuzzy appearance - most other willowherbs like cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb are greener with less conspicuous hairs. The small flowers and compact size also distinguish it from the tall, showy great willowherb.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's willowherbs, cinnamon willowherb is distinguished by its colorful stems and leaves - most other willowherbs stay green throughout the season.
Among New England's willowherbs, great willowherb lives up to its name by being the tallest and most robust.
Among New England's willowherbs, fringed willowherb is distinguished by those characteristic tiny hairs along its leaf edges - no other local willowherb has this feature.
Unlike its lowland cousins like great willowherb or cinnamon willowherb, Hornemann's willowherb is much smaller in all respects - shorter stems, tinier flowers, and narrower leaves.
Among New England's willowherbs, linear-leaf willowherb has the narrowest leaves and prefers the wettest habitats.
Among New England's willowherbs, downy willowherb is distinguished by its thoroughly fuzzy texture - much more so than cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb.
Marsh willowherb is much smaller and more delicate than Great Willowherb, which can tower over 6 feet tall with showy magenta flowers.
